#Package Download and Data-cleaning

# Load in all necessary packages
```{r}
library(TCGAbiolinks)
library(sesame)
library(sesameData)
library(limma)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Query, Download, and Prepare the data.
```{r}
query <- GDCquery(project = "TCGA-BRCA",
                  data.category = "DNA Methylation",
                  data.type = "Methylation Beta Value",
                  platform = "Illumina Human Methylation 450",
                  data.format = "Dataframe")
```

```{r}
GDCdownload(query) 
```

```{r}
methylation450 <- GDCprepare(query)
```

The above data requires a LOT of memory. My recommendation: GDCdownload() and GDCprepare() in separate R sessions.
R requires a lot of memory for both.

```{r}
methylation_clinical <- as.data.frame(methylation450@colData)
betas <- as.data.frame(methylation450@assays@data@listData) #takes a longer time
cpg_sites <- as.data.frame(methylation450@rowRanges@elementMetadata)

column_mask <- ifelse(colnames(methylation_clinical) %in% c('treatments', 'primary_site', 'disease_type','sites_of_involvement'), F, T)

methylation_clinical <- methylation_clinical[,column_mask]
write.csv(methylation_clinical, 'brca_methylation_clinical.csv')


site_mask <- !grepl('-', cpg_sites$gene) & !grepl(';', cpg_sites$gene) & !is.na(cpg_sites$gene) & complete.cases(betas)
betas <- betas[site_mask,]
cpg_sites <- cpg_sites[site_mask,]

write.csv(betas, 'brca_methylation_betas.csv') #takes a longer time
write.csv(cpg_sites, 'brca_cpg_sites.csv')
```

Use the code below if you are loading in your data (i.e. you downloaded the data and closed the session, but you are back to continue working)
```{r}
methylation_clinical <- read.csv('brca_methylation_clinical.csv', row.names = 1)
betas <- read.csv('brca_methylation_betas.csv', row.names=1)
cpg_sites <- read.csv('brca_cpg_sites.csv', row.names = 1)
```


# (1) Naive Differential Methylation
```{r}
#masking out NAs
metastasis_mask <- methylation_clinical$definition %in% c("Metastatic", "Primary solid Tumor")
methylation_clinical <- methylation_clinical[metastasis_mask, ]
betas_clean <- betas[, metastasis_mask]

#creating our variable of interest & deciding the base group
methylation_clinical$metastasis_category <- ifelse(methylation_clinical$definition== "Metastatic", "metastatic", "primary")

#define your comparison and base group
primary_mask <- methylation_clinical$metastasis_category == "primary"
methylation_clinical$metastatic <- !primary_mask #old is comparison, young is base

#fitting linear models using a "target value"
mval <- t(apply(betas_clean, 1, function(x) log2(x/(1-x)))) 
#mvalue is another statistic for methylation, centered at 0 and ranges from -1 to 1
#this step will take a few seconds to run

design <- model.matrix(~ metastatic, data = methylation_clinical)
fit <- lmFit(mval, design)
fit2 <- eBayes(fit)
```

```{r}
# Extracting model into dataframe
dat <- data.frame(foldchange = fit[["coefficients"]][,2], logPvalue =  -log10(p.adjust(fit2[["p.value"]][,2],method='BY')), geneName = cpg_sites$gene)
dat$threshold <- as.factor(abs(dat$foldchange) < 1)

# Visualization
cols <- c("TRUE" = "grey", "FALSE" = "blue")
ggplot(data=dat, aes(x=foldchange, y = logPvalue)) +
  geom_point(alpha=.2, size=0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cols) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour="#990000", linetype="dashed") + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = - 1, colour="#990000", linetype="dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 2, colour = "#990000", linetype="dashed") +
  theme(legend.position="none") +
  xlab("Fold Change") +
  ylab("-log10 p value") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# Saving results to a .csv file
write.csv(dat, "methylation_results_metastasis.csv")
```

#What conclusions can you draw about diff. between metastatic and non-metastatic TCGA BRACA patients? 

->from the volcano plot we can infer that there are several DNA sites that are significantly more or less (when looking at the negative and postitive folds) methylated when comparing metastatic to primary breast cancer patients. However, we cannot conclude whether these epigentic alteration directly result in or drive the progression of cancer. This is because the limitation in the observational comparison which only allows for correlation rather than causation analysis.This is because the plot does not consider other biological variable. 



#(2) Direct comparison of methylation status to transcriptional activity
...INSERT DESeq2 Stuff here to generate 'results'...

```{r}
de_results <- read.csv("../490_cluster/analysis_data/brca_deseq2_results.csv")

rna_clinical <- read.csv("../490_cluster/analysis_data/brca_rna_clinical_data.csv", row.names = 1)
rna_genes <- read.csv("../490_cluster/analysis_data/brca_rna_gene_data.csv")
rna_counts <- read.csv("../490_cluster/analysis_data/brca_rna_count_data.csv", row.names = 1)
```

```{r}

de_results$gene_id_clean <- sub("\\\\..*", "", de_results$X)
rna_genes$gene_id_clean <- sub("\\\\..*", "", rna_genes$gene_id) 


de_results_mapped <- merge(de_results, rna_genes, by.x = "gene_id_clean", by.y = "gene_id_clean")
downregulated <- de_results_mapped[(de_results_mapped$log2FoldChange < -1 & !is.na(de_results_mapped$padj) & de_results_mapped$padj < 0.05), 'gene_name']
hypermethylated <- dat[dat$foldchange > 1.5, 'geneName'] #What cutoff should you use -> cutoff of 1.5 because it successfully filters for highly hypermethylated genes.


interest_genes <- intersect(downregulated, hypermethylated)
print(interest_genes)

```

```{r}

interest_genes <- c("FGFR1")
GENE <- "FGFR1"

gene_counts_mask <- rna_genes$gene_name == GENE
gene_betas_mask <- cpg_sites$gene == GENE

#What are we doing here? -> creating column masks to separate your patients and samples by disease stage (Metastatic vs. Non)
rna_metastatic_mask <- rna_clinical$definition == "Metastatic"
rna_primary_mask <- rna_clinical$definition == "Primary solid Tumor"

meth_metastatic_mask <- methylation_clinical$metastasis_category == "metastatic"
meth_primary_mask <- methylation_clinical$metastasis_category == "primary"

#What are we doing here? -> extracting the final data from DNAH10, turning RNA data into numerical imputs (1 dimensional) and methylation into matrices (2 dimensional) inputs 
rna_metastatic <- as.numeric(rna_counts[gene_counts_mask, rna_metastatic_mask])
rna_primary <- as.numeric(rna_counts[gene_counts_mask, rna_primary_mask])


methylation_metastatic <- betas_clean[gene_betas_mask, meth_metastatic_mask, drop = FALSE]
methylation_primary <- betas_clean[gene_betas_mask, meth_primary_mask, drop = FALSE]

```

```{r}

boxplot(rna_primary, rna_metastatic, 
        xlab = 'Group', 
        ylab = 'Counts', 
        names = c('Primary', 'Metastatic'),
        col = c("blue", "red"),
        main = paste("Expression of", GENE))
```
```{r}
plot(1:nrow(methylation_primary), apply(methylation_primary, 1, mean, na.rm = TRUE), 
     col = 'blue', type = 'h', lwd = 3, 
     ylab = 'Average Beta', xlab = 'CpG sites',
     main = paste("Methylation Profiles of", GENE))

lines(1.3:(nrow(methylation_metastatic) + 0.3), apply(methylation_metastatic, 1, mean, na.rm = TRUE), 
      col = 'red', type = 'h', lwd = 3)

legend("topright",
       legend = c("Primary", "Metastatic"),
       col = c("blue", "red"),
       lwd = 3,
       cex = 0.7)
```

#Direct comparison of methylation status to transcriptional activity across non-metastatic vs. metastatic patients in 1 gene of interest (Box plot & bar plot): 

When looking at the box plot and bar plot we can identify that FGFR1 is hypermethylated (red bar higher than blue in sites 12, 13, 14 in the bar plot) and down regulated (box plot showing metastatic cohorts suppression of highly expressing outlier in the population) in metastatic patients. FGFR1 shows a higher ave. methylation across the CpG sites and a decrease in transcriptional expression (metastatic compared to primary). However we cannot conclude that the DNA hypermethylation directly results in turning off this gene or the silencing of FGR1 directly correlates cancer metastasis. Again the plot only demonstrate the correlation between increased methylation and decreased gene expression, without adressing other variables like other regulatory factors or proving a direct causal role in tumor progression.
